title: “WHY DO YOU CALL ME ‘LORD, LORD’… AND STILL IGNORE ME?”
paragraphs:
“WHY DO YOU CALL ME ‘LORD, LORD’… AND STILL IGNORE ME?”
The terrifying question Jesus asked religious people—and the difference between knowing His name and actually surrendering your life to Him.
There are words of Jesus that comfort you.
And then there are words of Jesus that corner you.
Words that leave nowhere to hide.
No Bible verse in your biography.
No cross hanging around your neck.
“Why do you call Me ‘Lord, Lord,’ and not do what I say?”
That question appears in Luke 6:46, and perhaps we have heard it so many times that we no longer feel how devastating it actually is.
But imagine hearing it from Christ Himself.
Not from someone trying to shame you.
Not from someone who knows only the public version of your life.
The One who knows what happens after everyone else goes home.
The One who knows what you delete.
What you keep promising to surrender.
What you know He has told you…
and what you continue refusing to do.
The Greek text preserves the force of His question:
Τί δέ με καλεῖτε· Κύριε κύριε, καὶ οὐ ποιεῖτε ἃ λέγω;
Ti de me kaleite, Kyrie kyrie, kai ou poieite ha legō?
“Why do you call Me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ and not do what I say?”
That repeated Κύριε κύριε—Kyrie, kyrie—“Lord, Lord” matters.
Jesus is confronting an unbearable contradiction between confession and conduct.
Their mouths are saying one thing.
And suddenly Christianity becomes painfully personal.
Because it is possible to say “Lord” beautifully…
while quietly living as though you are lord.
We can sing about surrender while negotiating the terms of our obedience.
We can raise our hands on Sunday while holding tightly to the very thing Christ has commanded us to release.
We can post Scripture publicly and entertain sin privately.
We can defend biblical truth in comment sections while refusing to practice biblical forgiveness in our own homes.
We can tell the world that Jesus is King while treating His commands as suggestions to be followed whenever they agree with our feelings.
Why do you call Me Lord?
The word κύριος—kyrios can mean “lord,” “master,” or one possessing authority.
So calling Jesus “Lord” is not merely attaching a religious title to His name.
If He is Lord, I am not.
If He is Master, I do not get to rewrite His commands whenever obedience becomes uncomfortable.
If He is King, Christianity cannot merely be Jesus decorating the life I already wanted.
And that is precisely where Christianity becomes more uncomfortable than religious culture sometimes allows.
Because many people want Jesus as Savior without wanting Jesus as Lord.
We want Christ to rescue us from hell while leaving the throne of our present life untouched.
But the biblical Jesus does not merely offer improvement.
He calls us to follow Him.
It means when Jesus goes one direction and my sinful desires go another, somebody has to lose.
Biblical repentance means I stop insisting that somebody must always be Jesus.
This is why Luke 6:46 cannot be ripped out of its context and turned into a slogan about “trying harder.”
He says that the person who comes to Him, hears His words, and does them is like a man building a house who dug deep and laid its foundation upon rock.
The river slammed against the house.
But it could not shake it because it had been well built.
The foolish person is not ignorant of the words.
But he does not act upon them.
Jesus says this person resembles someone who builds a house on the ground without a foundation.
Jesus concludes that its ruin is great.
The dividing line was not exposure to Jesus' teaching.
It was what they did after hearing it.
That means one of the greatest dangers in Christianity is becoming so familiar with truth that familiarity begins impersonating obedience.
You know when to say amen.
You may even know enough theology to correct somebody else's doctrine.
But knowing what Jesus said and submitting to what Jesus said are not identical things.
James later expresses the same danger:
“Be doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving yourselves.”
There is a kind of deception that does not require somebody else lying to you.
You can do it to yourself.
You can mistake conviction for repentance.
You can feel guilty and assume you have changed.
You can cry during worship and assume tears equal surrender.
You can agree with a sermon and assume agreement equals obedience.
You can know that something is wrong…
promise God you will never do it again…
and still protect the doorway through which you keep returning to it.
Jesus is not asking whether His words moved you emotionally.
He is asking whether His words moved you obediently.
And before anyone turns this into salvation by moral performance, we need to hear the rest of the Gospel.
Because Jesus did not come looking for people who had already achieved flawless obedience.
If that were the requirement for approaching Him, nobody would come.
“All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.”
The woman caught in adultery stood exposed.
The thief beside Jesus was literally dying under criminal condemnation.
Christianity is not the announcement that good people successfully climbed their way to God.
Christianity is the announcement that God came down to sinners.
Jesus Christ lived the righteousness we have failed to live.
He went willingly to the cross.
The answer to hypocrisy is therefore not pretending harder.
It is coming into the light.
“Jesus, I have called You Lord with my mouth while fighting Your authority with my life.”
And here is where scandal begins becoming grace.
Because the same Christ who exposes hypocrisy also receives repentant sinners.
Jesus does not expose you because He enjoys humiliation.
He exposes what is killing you because darkness survives by remaining hidden.
Grace does not say your rebellion does not matter.
Grace says your rebellion mattered enough that Christ went to the cross—and His mercy is greater than the sin you finally stop defending.
He said he would never abandon Jesus.
Then, within hours, he denied even knowing Him.
The collapse of everything Peter thought he was.
Yet Peter's scandal was not the final chapter.
After the resurrection, Jesus restored him.
Not because denial suddenly became acceptable.
Not because truth no longer mattered.
But because failure surrendered to Christ does not have to become your identity forever.
That does not mean He calls evil good.
It means He takes sinners who have finally stopped pretending and begins transforming them by grace.
That is the Gospel Warrior heartbeat:
Not from scandal to pretending the scandal never happened.
Not from scandal to religious reputation management.
Your friends would never suspect it.
Maybe there is an addiction behind the worship songs.
A secret relationship behind the Christian image.
Greed behind the generosity people see.
Unforgiveness buried beneath years of religious language.
Or maybe your rebellion looks respectable.
That can be even harder to recognize.
Maybe you are not living in some spectacular public scandal.
Maybe you simply keep telling Jesus:
Later I will surrender this relationship.
Later I will seek God seriously.
Later I will become the person Christ is calling me to become.
But delayed obedience can become dressed-up disobedience.
if you have already decided which commands you will ignore?
And this is where the article stops being about “those hypocritical Christians.”
What has Jesus already made clear that you keep negotiating?
What are you defending that Scripture is confronting?
Who are you refusing to forgive?
What relationship has become more authoritative than Christ?
What appetite gets the final vote?
What command do you secretly wish Jesus had never given?
Because sometimes the command that irritates us most reveals the throne we are protecting most fiercely.
And perhaps right now you feel exposed.
The enemy wants exposure to drive you away from Christ in shame.
The Gospel calls exposed sinners toward Christ in repentance.
Romans 8:1 declares that there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.
That promise is not permission to make peace with sin.
It is freedom to stop hiding from the Savior.
You don't have to clean yourself perfectly before approaching Jesus.
The thing you said you would never do again.
The thing you are ashamed to name.
But don't bring it so you can ask Jesus to bless it.
Bring it so you can surrender it.
Jesus does not merely want to become another voice in your life.
And genuine faith does not produce sinless perfection overnight, but it does change our relationship with obedience.
The Christian still fights the flesh.
We stop making peace treaties with the sins Christ died to redeem us from.
We discover another room in our hearts that we have kept locked…
and eventually hand Him the key.
Living because we have received it.
“If you love Me, keep My commandments.”
Obedience is not the price we pay to purchase His grace.
Obedience is fruit growing from a life captured by His grace.
You cannot accumulate enough Christian achievements to make God indebted to you.
Yet the grace that forgives also transforms.
Christ does not merely pardon rebels and leave rebellion enthroned.
So maybe tonight your prayer does not need sophisticated theology.
Forgive me for the places where I have only called You Lord.
Show me where my confession and my life contradict each other.
Give me strength to obey where I have been resisting.
Forgive whom Christ commands you to forgive.
Seek wise, mature Christian accountability where you need help.
Not because these actions purchase salvation.
Because when the King calls, disciples follow.
If you have spent years performing Christianity while secretly starving spiritually?
And repentance is still one of God's great mercies because it means your present direction does not have to become your final destination.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you don't have to tell strangers every private detail. But you can refuse to hide from God anymore.
Sometimes one honest sentence is where the mask finally begins to crack.
Not because sharing a Facebook article earns favor with God. It doesn't.
But if biblical truth has helped you, sharing it can place that truth in front of someone you may never realize is quietly drowning.
Send it privately to the friend whose faith has gone cold.
Invite the believer who is struggling.
Invite the person who has been wounded by religious hypocrisy.
Invite even the person who says they no longer believe.
Let them encounter Christ rather than another performance of Christianity.
Because one day the storm may hit your own house, and you may need to remember what Jesus said about foundations.
Your support helps us keep creating Scripture-centered content intended to point people toward Jesus, repentance, grace, forgiveness, redemption, and transformed lives.

Not to become another follower on a page.
The question was never merely whether your lips could pronounce the word “Lord.”
The question is whether the One you call Lord actually has your life.
Because eventually every house meets a storm.
And when the waters rise, the foundation underneath everything you have built will matter far more than the Christian name painted across the front door.
“Why do you call Me ‘Lord, Lord,’ and not do what I say?”
don't waste the question by applying it only to somebody else.
Let it bring you to repentance.
Then let grace lead you home.
The most dangerous distance in Christianity may be the few inches between a mouth that says “Lord” and a heart that still whispers, “I will rule myself.”
